articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India should use multilateral fora to advance bilateral cooperation

While maintaining its hard stance on cross-border terrorism, India has an opportunity to recognise that many of its other interests still merit sustained cooperation with Pakistan as the latter’s climate minister Musadik Masood Malik prepares to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi. India’s official position since the Pahalgam attack and the ensuing confrontations along the border is that terrorism and bilateral talks cannot coexist. A month later, Prime Minister Narendra Modi signalled that India’s relations with Pakistan would remain subordinate to its demands on cross-border terrorism by extending the condition to trade and water. South Asia is already one of the least economically integrated regions worldwide, with intra-regional trade at around 5%, and, as Chatham House has inferred, strained ties between India and its neighbours have created diplomatic vacuums that Beijing has taken advantage of through trilateral and regional groupings. Now, by inviting all SCO members to the national capital and participating in meetings ahead of the August 2027 Islamabad Summit, New Delhi has shown some maturity as a convening power. Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Mr. Modi.

The pursuit of regionwide water security remains particularly fluid, with India seemingly overlooking the fact that it is upstream of Pakistan and Bangladesh and downstream of China. After India stopped sharing routine hydrological data of the Indus river and approved the Chenab-Beas link tunnel project, Mr. Malik fanned the flames saying Pakistan would “cut off those hands” seeking to restrict its share of the water. Yet China has now restricted the same data vis-à-vis the Brahmaputra while it builds the Medog mega-dam in Tibet. India has also protested the proposed Padma Barrage in Bangladesh, which has been increasing its alignment with China, echoing India building the Farakka Barrage over East Pakistan’s objections in 1961. Climate change is rendering cooperation more essential to manage the integrity of contested geographies, the willingness of border populations to engage, and the potential to generate hydroelectric power. New Delhi should retreat from the notion that working together on the Indus will be a concession to Islamabad and see in the Dialogue an opportunity to restore the necessary channels. Suspending ties may communicate political resolve but will not diminish terrorists’ capabilities in the region or improve India’s security. It has already compromised India’s ambitions to regional leadership, which require the ability to keep engaging even with difficult neighbours. India should go beyond using multilateral fora to assert its national position and start identifying areas where bilateral cooperation serves its interests, including with Pakistan.

articles.title: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The dangers of centralising the internet’s architecture are now clear

Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

Editorial Context: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.
• Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

articles.title: Stoop to conquer: On the Opposition’s seat-sharing ahead of U.P. polls
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The Congress should scale down its ambition while seeking an alliance with the SP

As Uttar Pradesh heads to the polls in early 2027, a familiar seat-sharing tussle has emerged within the Opposition. The Samajwadi Party and the Congress share an understanding forged during the Lok Sabha elections that earned them a good share of the State’s seats, but the Congress is now reportedly seeking 181 seats , nearly 45% of the 403 Assembly constituencies. It is the latest instance of the dilemma facing the Congress as it seeks revival in States where it has become a marginal force: how to strike a favourable bargain with stronger partners without weakening the coalition against the Bharatiya Janata Party. With discontent rising against the BJP, which still occupies a hegemonic position in the party system , the Opposition feels a wind behind its sails, and its major parties agree that the only way to take on the BJP is a formidable coalition with a compelling, unified message. But the Congress’s attempt to rebuild itself in the Hindi heartland and in States where it once held sway has strained that unity. In Bihar, the Mahagathbandhan failed to reap the benefits of anti-incumbency against the Janata Dal (United)-BJP alliance, partly because it could not tap the full support of the social forces behind the Rashtriya Janata Dal and the Congress, and partly because the Congress took too long to settle seat-sharing for the campaigns to gel. In Tamil Nadu, the Congress held out for more seats from the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam and delayed the alliance, while infighting produced a lacklustre campaign that left it with the lowest vote share, in the seats it contested, among the alliance partners.

Uttar Pradesh need not go the same way. The demand for 181 seats is overly ambitious for a party that managed a mere 2.33% of the votes in the 399 seats it contested in 2022, when the SP won 111 of the 347 seats it contested with a 32% vote share. The Congress has a point that the variables have changed since. In 2024, the SP and the Congress together won 43 of U.P.‘s 80 Lok Sabha seats with a 43.2% vote share, just short of the BJP-led alliance’s 43.7%. The Congress won only six of the 17 seats it contested, but its vote share in those six, 44.2%, was marginally ahead of the SP’s 43.4%. The party could also argue that its national campaigns on youth concerns and the state of India’s electoral democracy give it the heft to seek more. But its lack of an efficient State-wide organisation suggests that 181 is too high. The SP remains the strongest Opposition party , having assiduously built a new social coalition of backward classes, Dalits and minorities to take on the majoritarian BJP through local mobilisations. The 2024 arrangement, in which the Congress contested a fifth of the seats, is a more reasonable guide. A well-targeted 100 or so seats would make for a more coherent campaign and a better showing alongside the SP.

articles.title: Brace for impact: On rising inflation and external factors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: High inflation due to external factors could soon exacerbate economic pain

India’s much-hyped domestic economic resilience is set to be tested over the next few months as external factors start to impose inescapable pressures. A case in point is inflation. The latest data on retail inflation show that it crossed the Reserve Bank of India’s 6% upper comfort limit in October 2026. According to economists, this is likely to continue through the third quarter of this financial year, which means at least two more months of high inflation. Agricultural shortfalls brought on by a patchy and deficient monsoon have meant that food inflation rose sharply to 8.5% in October 2026. Elevated fuel prices meant that inflation in the transport category also rose sharply. What is worse is that high inflation is spreading to almost every aspect of a household’s day-to-day needs. In fact, the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) data show that 10 of the 12 major categories saw inflation in October, hitting their highest levels recorded in the new series of the index. So, things such as clothing, footwear, housing, furnishings, and services such as healthcare, education, communication, recreation, and restaurant and hospitality are not only getting more expensive, but they are doing so at an accelerating rate. This would have been bad enough had wages been increasing in real terms. Yet, the latest research by Data for India on the country’s official wage statistics shows that, while nominal wages doubled from 2012 to 2024, they actually fell 4% over the same period after adjusting for inflation. And this is sharper for high-skilled and high-earning workers. Lower wage earners saw marginal increases over this period. While this is of some comfort, it is the higher wage earners that drive consumption in an economy. Real wage contraction for them, which is likely to have worsened in 2026, will hit consumption levels and private investment.

Further, there is strong evidence to suggest that the official inflation metrics are not capturing the full extent of rising prices. Data on cash with the public and UPI transactions show the value of both has been growing in double digits over the last year and more, significantly outpacing nominal GDP growth. This either suggests that the informal economy is far larger than earlier thought or, more likely, that inflation is well above what the official figures are being able to capture. Unfortunately, there are no real magic-wand fixes to this situation. Inflation is largely beyond the government’s control, and wage growth cannot happen overnight. The only way forward is to continue trying to spur sector-specific growth and warn people of the impending storm.

articles.title: Critical ban: On recycling of lithium-ion batteries
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India needs to create an entire ecosystem for recycling of lithium-ion batteries

On November 10, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass by moving it from the “free” to the “prohibited” list of exports. Black mass is an intermediate product when spent batteries and factory scrap are shredded. It contains valuable lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. The Commerce Ministry says the ban will ensure feedstock for domestic refiners, lift their capacity utilisation and draw investment. While the recycling of lead-acid batteries end-to-end is an established ecosystem and formalised, too, lithium-ion battery recycling is an emerging segment with only a few dozen licensed operators but has much potential given the scale of use of such batteries in EVs. While the ban will redirect supply, it will not automatically create a market and ecosystem. Just banning export without creating an entire ecosystem will only lead to dumping of lithium-ion batteries into landfills if the blackmass has no market. Blackmass production is a largely mechanical process but further downstream processing is more specialised chemical processing requiring larger investment and further policy support. If downstream units are online, their output can directly feed into indigenous lithium-ion battery manufacture.

India depends heavily on imports for critical minerals such as those used in battery inputs. Beyond working on supply aspects, the government must address the price gap to create a robust recycling market. Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, producers buy extended producer responsibility (EPR) certificates from recyclers but these are undervalued. Cheap certificates reward recycling on paper over investment in high-yield plants. A floor price that covers the full cost of recovery, with digital tracking, would fix that. Rare earths show how recycling remains a missed opportunity for India because of policy gaps. A smartphone can be up to 1% neodymium-iron-boron magnet by weight. That puts its rare earth content at about 3,000 parts per million, comparable to India’s monazite beach sands. Extracting it takes less energy than mining. A magnet separated from the phone is about 30% rare earth. Magnets make up as much as 3% of a hard drive, but are usable only if they are removed before the drive is shredded for data destruction. Yet the e-waste rules do not require rare earth separation. Rare earths need a separate EPR category, too. Payment by weight cannot be applied for rare earth minerals.

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

India needs to create an entire ecosystem for recycling of lithium-ion batteries

On November 10, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass by moving it from the “free” to the “prohibited” list of exports. Black mass is an intermediate product when spent batteries and factory scrap are shredded. It contains valuable lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. The Commerce Ministry says the ban will ensure feedstock for domestic refiners, lift their capacity utilisation and draw investment. While the recycling of lead-acid batteries end-to-end is an established ecosystem and formalised, too, lithium-ion battery recycling is an emerging segment with only a few dozen licensed operators but has much potential given the scale of use of such batteries in EVs. While the ban will redirect supply, it will not automatically create a market and ecosystem. Just banning export without creating an entire ecosystem will only lead to dumping of lithium-ion batteries into landfills if the blackmass has no market. Blackmass production is a largely mechanical process but further downstream processing is more specialised chemical processing requiring larger investment and further policy support. If downstream units are online, their output can directly feed into indigenous lithium-ion battery manufacture.

India depends heavily on imports for critical minerals such as those used in battery inputs. Beyond working on supply aspects, the government must address the price gap to create a robust recycling market. Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, producers buy extended producer responsibility (EPR) certificates from recyclers but these are undervalued. Cheap certificates reward recycling on paper over investment in high-yield plants. A floor price that covers the full cost of recovery, with digital tracking, would fix that. Rare earths show how recycling remains a missed opportunity for India because of policy gaps. A smartphone can be up to 1% neodymium-iron-boron magnet by weight. That puts its rare earth content at about 3,000 parts per million, comparable to India’s monazite beach sands. Extracting it takes less energy than mining. A magnet separated from the phone is about 30% rare earth. Magnets make up as much as 3% of a hard drive, but are usable only if they are removed before the drive is shredded for data destruction. Yet the e-waste rules do not require rare earth separation. Rare earths need a separate EPR category, too. Payment by weight cannot be applied for rare earth minerals.

fullParagraphs: Three Maoist dumps comprising around 280 Barrel Grenade Launcher (BGL) shells were recovered by a joint team of Charla police, Bomb Disposal Squad personnel and Special Party police from a forest area along the Telangana-Chhattisgarh border near Karregutta hills on Monday.
The recovery was made based on information provided by some surrendered Maoists, police said.

Police suspect that the Maoists had concealed the BGL shells in the forest belt, once considered one of their strongholds, in early 2025 for future use.

Several Maoist cadres surrendered before the Telangana police in late 2025 and early 2026, reportedly influenced by the State government’s surrender and rehabilitation policy and expressing a willingness to return to mainstream society, police added.

articles.title: Youth urged to focus on current affairs for competitive examinations
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Dr BR Ambedkar University former Vice-Chancellor Hanumanthu Lajapathirai on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) urged youngsters preparing for competitive examinations to focus on current affairs by reading newspapers in a systematic way. He said the students should focus on issues related to international affairs, new government policies, sports, agriculture, and economy.

Along with Forest Range Officer Birlangi Ram Naresh, he inaugurated the seminar on “How and what to read in newspapers-youngsters preparing for competitive examinations,” organised by Vizianagaram Reads Founder Repalle Eswara Rao in connection with the 59th Library Week celebrations held in Vizianagaram.

Speaking on the occasion, he said that the students should not focus on regular political developments since those would not help during competitive examinations. “Newspapers like The Hindu help students have a comprehensive outlook on all important issues with their editorials, exclusive international, and sports pages,” said Dr. Lajapathirai.
Mr. Ram Naresh said that the students should spend more time in libraries and prepare their own notes in a systematic way.

Vizianagaram Reads Founder Repalle Eswara Rao said that his association was inculcating reading habits among the children, making them visit libraries on Sundays and holidays. The association mentor Naveen Polipalli and others were present.

articles.title: Karnataka: Farmers may have to wait a year or more to grow new crop varieties of ragi, maize and amaranth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: These new varieties include Ragi GPU 101 which is an improved variety of MR-322, Maize MAH-20-45, an improved variety of MAH-14-5, and Grain Amaranth KBGA-18, an improved variety of KBGA-15.

In light of the drought issue across Karnataka, three new crop varieties of ragi, maize and grain amaranth developed at the University of Agriculture Sciences-Bengaluru (UAS-B) were launched at the ongoing Krishi Mela. However, scientists who were involved in developing these varieties, as well as experts from other institutions, stated that it would take a year or two for these varieties to be available in the market for farmers to purchase.

These new varieties include Ragi GPU 101 which is an improved variety of MR-322, Maize MAH-20-45, an improved variety of MAH-14-5, and Grain Amaranth KBGA-18, an improved variety of KBGA-15. Scientists said that even before these varieties reach the market, it would take time to multiply seeds in large numbers, test them in various locations and weather conditions, get the varieties notified and approved by the respective organisations at the national and State levels.

Mudalagiriyappa D.R., Director of Research at UAS-B, said, “Though the new varieties have been launched, they are not available for farmers to purchase from the open market and cultivate. It will take a year or more for these crop varieties to be made fully available to the farmers in large numbers. A national indent has to be placed by the Ministry of Agriculture so that seeds of these crop varieties can be multiplied and made available to farmers across the country.”

Meanwhile, Sujata Bhat, Senior Technical Assistant, UAS-B, also stated that it took nearly 13 years for the university to develop Ragi GPU-101. Pointing towards the fresh yield of GPU-101 exhibited at Krishi Mela, she said, “The yield is 27% more when compared to the yield in the existing variety MR-322. But it has to be tested successfully for private companies to come forward and multiply seeds in large numbers.”

Uday Kumar, technical manager at the Institute of Agricultural Technologists, said, “The National Seed Corporation (NSC) under the government of India will take up large-scale multiplication of improved and notified crop varieties. Anything that the Ministry of Agriculture notifies, those varieties will be multiplied by NSC and sold to the farmers. Agriculture universities have fund constraints and can multiply the seeds only by a few hundred kilograms instead of tonnes. They must proactively market the seeds and its information once approved by the Ministry of Agriculture. Only then will private companies also come forward to multiply and sell them on a large scale.”

He also noted that the university and the State Agriculture Department must work in coordination to forecast drought conditions, El Nino impact and crops that farmers are supposed to cultivate during such conditions. “If the forecasting is perfect then such crop varieties can be tested and released in large quantities,” he added.

articles.title: Land transfer clears way for road widening near Kothagudem Railway Station
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Alternate land handed over to Railways to create parking facility at Khammam Railway Station

Khammam MP R. Raghuram Reddy has said that the process of transferring 5,500 square yards of railway land to the State government for widening the road near Kothagudem (Bhadrachalam Road) railway station in Bhadradri Kothagudem district has been completed.

Speaking to the media in Khammam on Tuesday (November 17), Mr. Reddy said local residents had been demanding the widening of the narrow road stretch near the Kothagudem Railway Station for the past 20 years to ease traffic congestion.
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy had held discussions with the Union Railway Minister and sought the transfer of railway land in Kothagudem to facilitate the proposed road widening.
“Following our sustained efforts, the documentation for transferring the railway land to the State government has been completed, paving the way for the long-pending road widening project,” he said.

In return, the State government had issued a Government Order (GO) for transferring 4,400 square yards of government land near the Khammam Railway Station to the Railways to facilitate the development of parking facilities, he added.

Mr. Reddy said district officials had taken necessary precautions to ensure that shops near Khammam railway station would not suffer any loss as a result of the transfer of government land to the Railways.

Alternate land handed over to Railways to create parking facility at Khammam Railway Station

Khammam MP R. Raghuram Reddy has said that the process of transferring 5,500 square yards of railway land to the State government for widening the road near Kothagudem (Bhadrachalam Road) railway station in Bhadradri Kothagudem district has been completed.

Speaking to the media in Khammam on Tuesday (November 17), Mr. Reddy said local residents had been demanding the widening of the narrow road stretch near the Kothagudem Railway Station for the past 20 years to ease traffic congestion.

Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy had held discussions with the Union Railway Minister and sought the transfer of railway land in Kothagudem to facilitate the proposed road widening.

“Following our sustained efforts, the documentation for transferring the railway land to the State government has been completed, paving the way for the long-pending road widening project,” he said.

In return, the State government had issued a Government Order (GO) for transferring 4,400 square yards of government land near the Khammam Railway Station to the Railways to facilitate the development of parking facilities, he added.

Mr. Reddy said district officials had taken necessary precautions to ensure that shops near Khammam railway station would not suffer any loss as a result of the transfer of government land to the Railways.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes

She joined YSRCP as she was not happy with undemocratic approaches in the TDP. Our combined personal vote bank and support from all sections of the society will help us win the Mayor seat as well as majority wards out of 60 in the corporation limits,” he added.

articles.title: Rising prices reflect government’s economic mismanagement: Congress
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Monthly costs up by over 20% for 61% of families, according to a survey cited by Congress leader Jairam Ramesh; claims PM is more pre-occupied with politics than tackling the inflation crisis

The Congress on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) accused the Union government of fuelling inflation through its “economic mismanagement and anti-people policies” and alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi remained preoccupied with politics rather than addressing the economic distress faced by households and businesses.

Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh cited a survey which found that, for 61% of families across the country, monthly household expenditure had risen by more than 20% over the past year. While 74% of respondents were cutting back on non-essential spending, 50% had reduced purchases of essential goods, he said.
Citing the survey, Mr. Ramesh said prices of ghee and edible oils had risen by 75%, vegetables by 73%, cereals by 71%, milk and dairy products by 65%, and pulses by 62%.

He also claimed that 200 garment factories had shut down in Noida over the past year, citing the impact of U.S. tariffs, high input costs, and government apathy. He said the closures reflected the wider distress in the textile industry.

“People’s plates are shrinking, and factories are being locked down. Yet, the Prime Minister’s only concern remains politics,” he said on X, accusing the government of failing to acknowledge people’s hardships or offer relief.

articles.title: A poverty line that falls short
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Reliable poverty estimates are not just for academic purposes. India has made real progress, but without a credible benchmark, it is hard to say how much, or how much remains to be done

There is no serious doubt that poverty in India has fallen sharply over the past decade. However, researchers and policymakers cannot agree on how many are still poor. Depending on the estimate, the share ranges from about 5% to more than 26%. Take the recent World Bank report. At its international line of $3 a day (2021 PPP), 2.6% of Indians were poor in 2022-23. Raise the line to $4.20, the bank’s benchmark for lower middle-income countries, and the figure jumps to around 16.1%. Same country, same year. Only the yardstick changed. A low level of extreme poverty does not necessarily mean poverty is not still a major issue. Where you draw the line decides how much economic insecurity you see.

India’s own figures tell a similar convoluted story. For example, SBI Research (2025) takes the Tendulkar line of 2009, adjusts it for inflation, and gets poverty of 7.2% in rural India and 4.6% in urban India for 2022-23. Rangarajan and Dev (2014), using an inflation-adjusted version of the Rangarajan Committee line, arrive at 10.8%. Further, Sethu, Surya and Ruthu (2024), who rebuild the Rangarajan method from the latest consumption survey, report 26.4%. Most of that gap boils down to the lines themselves: SBI’s Tendulkar-based lines use, after adjusting for inflation, about ₹1,632 a month per person in rural areas and ₹1,944 in urban areas. In contrast, Sethu et al. use much higher thresholds of ₹2,515 and ₹3,639. And the outcomes are obvious: Higher lines, higher poverty. Method matters too. One camp takes an old line and adjusts it for inflation. The other reconstructs the line from spending patterns in the new survey. Both have limitations, and they are answering different questions.
Macroeconomic & Financial Update: A poverty line that falls short. This development reflects key trends in India's fiscal roadmap, monetary policy transmission, and banking sector resilience.

articles.title: Export duty on diesel hiked ₹2.5/litre, ATF ₹1.5/litre, petrol remains nil
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The government late Monday (November 16, 2026) hiked the export duty on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) by ₹2.5 per litre and ₹1.5 per litre, whilst keeping the levy on export of petrol unchanged at nil.
Duty rates on petrol and diesel meant for domestic consumption remain unchanged.
The hike in diesel levy assumes added significance as India looks to further up their exports of the vehicular fuel to Europe amid a global supply crunch.
In the upcoming fortnight, diesel exports would draw a levy of ₹14 per litre compared to ₹11.5 per litre mandated for the previous fortnight.
ATF exports would draw a levy of ₹12.5 per litre against ₹11 per litre.

The government has been conducting a fortnightly review of export levies since March 27, in the backdrop of the conflict in West Asia. These are done based on the average international benchmark prices of crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF observed since the previous review.
This is to ensure the domestic availability of retail fuels by disincentivising exports.

The government late Monday (November 16, 2026) hiked the export duty on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) by ₹2.5 per litre and ₹1.5 per litre, whilst keeping the levy on export of petrol unchanged at nil.

Duty rates on petrol and diesel meant for domestic consumption remain unchanged.

The hike in diesel levy assumes added significance as India looks to further up their exports of the vehicular fuel to Europe amid a global supply crunch.

In the upcoming fortnight, diesel exports would draw a levy of ₹14 per litre compared to ₹11.5 per litre mandated for the previous fortnight.

ATF exports would draw a levy of ₹12.5 per litre against ₹11 per litre.

The government has been conducting a fortnightly review of export levies since March 27, in the backdrop of the conflict in West Asia. These are done based on the average international benchmark prices of crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF observed since the previous review.

articles.title: Wholesale inflation rises to 12.3% in October 2026, second straight month of double-digit inflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: According to economists, not only will this high wholesale inflation soon translate into higher consumer prices, but it also means an interest rate hike is nearly certain, which would dampen economic sentiment

Wholesale inflation in India surged to 12.3% in October 2026, the second consecutive month of double-digit inflation, official data released on Monday (November 16, 2026) showed. Fuel prices continue to be the main reason for the price rise, with the crude petroleum and natural gas sectors seeing inflation of more than 70%.

The new series of the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry has data that goes back to only April 2024 and so a historical analysis for a longer duration is not possible. However, the data shows that inflation in October was the highest since at least then.
This data follows the release of Consumer Price Index data last week that showed that even retail inflation had climbed above the Reserve Bank of India’s upper comfort mark of 6% in October 2026.
According to Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at the Bank of Baroda, it is only a matter of time before wholesale inflation translates into a further increase in the prices consumers pay.

“It has been seen that manufactured goods in particular have witnessed an increase of 9.5%, with high inflation rates in textiles, tobacco products, chemicals, rubber products, metals and electrical equipment,” Mr. Sabnavis pointed out. “This will pressurise companies into increasing their product prices at some point of time.”
“This passthrough will get reflected in the core part of the CPI in the coming months depending on the actions of industry,” he added.

Further, as Payal V. Pandya, vice president at Bajaj Broking Prive argues, the high WPI inflation makes a rate hike by the RBI in December a near certainty, which would have a further dampening effect on the economy.

“The sharp rise in WPI inflation to 12.39% in October 2026 reinforces the inflationary concerns already reflected in elevated retail inflation readings,” Payal V. Pandya, vice president at Bajaj Broking Prive said. “As a result, a rate hike by the RBI in the upcoming Monetary Policy Committee meeting [in December] now looks almost certain.”

“Higher interest rates may impact lending activity, investments, and consumption, while sentiment across the financial sector could remain under pressure,” Ms. Pandya added. “With geopolitical tensions resurfacing in the Russia-Ukraine region, risks to inflation and economic growth have become even more pronounced.”

Within the WPI, food inflation climbed to 8.3% in October 2026, the highest in 22 months. The overall fuel and power category saw inflation jump to nearly 33% in the same month, compared to about 26% in September 2026. These high levels were, however, also a result of a low base, since this segment of the WPI was in contraction for large parts of 2025.

articles.title: Iron ore capacity under-utilisation in major-producing states prompt concerns as India sets 2047 target
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: With India’s iron ore demand projected to rise to 772 million tonnes (MT) by 2047, miners in Odisha, the country’s largest iron ore reserve holder, are yet to utilise nearly 40% of their existing capacities, raising concerns over resource wastage and potential revenue losses.
The issue has come under judicial scrutiny, with both the Supreme Court earlier this month and the Odisha High Court in January flagging the underutilisation of mining capacities.

The Odisha High Court, while agreeing with petitioners who highlighted the sluggish operationalisation of mines despite environmental clearances, observed that the delay had resulted in an average annual revenue loss of ₹4,000 crore to the State.
However, industry sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, attributed the delays primarily to prolonged forest clearance procedures, which often exceed the stipulated 18-month timeframe.

Data cited by petitioner Citizens’ Action Forum (Bhubaneswar) show that of the 246 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of mining capacity granted environmental clearance in FY25, only around 159 MTPA had been operationalised.

Separately, data published by mining consultancy BigMint in June 2026 show that Odisha produced 158 MT of iron ore in FY26 against an environmentally cleared capacity of 278 MTPA, indicating capacity utilisation of nearly 60%.
The underutilised capacity is particularly significant as it largely involves hematite, which is among the highest-grade varieties of iron ore

The shortfall also raises questions over India’s continued dependence on imports. According to the Mines Ministry, the country imported 12.3 MT of iron ore in FY26, incurring an expenditure of ₹11,115 crore.

Odisha accounted for more than 50% of India’s domestic iron ore production during FY26. Chhattisgarh contributed around 17.1%, followed by Karnataka at 16.6%. Capacity utilisation in the two states – albeit with significantly lower volumes than Odisha – stood at 62% and 80%, respectively, according to calculations based on BigMint data.

In January, the Odisha High Court directed that mining rights be mandatorily transferred to state-owned National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC) to ensure “optimum utilisation of the mines” and “eradicate any burden on the government exchequer”.

The shortfall also raises questions over India’s continued dependence on imports. According to the Mines Ministry, the country imported 12.3 MT of iron ore in FY26, incurring an expenditure of ₹11,115 crore.

Odisha accounted for more than 50% of India’s domestic iron ore production during FY26. Chhattisgarh contributed around 17.1%, followed by Karnataka at 16.6%. Capacity utilisation in the two states – albeit with significantly lower volumes than Odisha – stood at 62% and 80%, respectively, according to calculations based on BigMint data.

In January, the Odisha High Court directed that mining rights be mandatorily transferred to state-owned National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC) to ensure “optimum utilisation of the mines” and “eradicate any burden on the government exchequer”.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes major Russian bridge with drones and missiles as aerial attacks escalate
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and to support troops on the front line

The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Mr. Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said.

articles.title: Iran targets Bahrain, slams 'fabricated' dirty-bomb report
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Mediator Qatar urged "all parties" to show restraint following an uptick in hostilities, with Bahrain targeted three times in five days after a lull in Iranian attacks on Gulf countries since September

Iran launched a fresh drone attack against Bahrain on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) and dismissed a report alleging a dirty-bomb plot against the United States, which President Donald Trump said he took "very seriously".

Mediator Qatar urged "all parties" to show restraint following an uptick in hostilities, with Bahrain targeted three times in five days after a lull in Iranian attacks on Gulf countries since September.

Mr. Trump was speaking after CNN cited seven anonymous U.S. officials as saying Iran was plotting to target senior administration figures with a "dirty" bomb, laced with chemical or radioactive materials.
"If there is [such a threat], they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before," Trump said after arriving for a summit in the Philippines.
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy."
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei dismissed the report as "fabricated".

"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations" including "the fabricated media narrative surrounding an alleged 'dirty bomb' propagated by CNN", he posted on X.
Mr. Baqaei also criticised a New York Times report questioning whether Iranian dams and water projects had military uses.
Earlier on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), explosions boomed across Bahrain's capital as a mobile-phone alert warned residents to seek safety.

Bahrain's armed forces said they "confronted, intercepted and destroyed a number of treacherous Iranian aerial attacks today... before they could achieve their objectives", while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they targeted a U.S.-operated radar system.

fullParagraphs: Quad is a ‘trusted partnership’ delivering solutions, says PM Modi

Amid the geopolitical tension, what the world needs today is peace, stability and predictability, Prime Minister Narendra Modi underlined at the ASEAN-India Summit, the East Asia Summit and the Quad Summit in Philippines, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri said.

Mr. Misri, in a briefing, said the Prime Minister has just completed a short but very intense visit to Manila, where he participated in the 23rd India-ASEAN Summit, the 21st East Asia Summit and the 7th Quad Leaders Summit.

At each of the three meetings, the Prime Minister underlined that in a world that has seen a great deal of geopolitical tension, flux and stresses and strains, what the world really needs today is peace, stability and predictability, Mr. Misri said.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi departed for New Delhi after concluding his two-day visit to the Philippines, during which he attended the ASEAN-India Summit, the East Asia Summit and a meeting of the Quad leaders.
Mr. Modi also met Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., and the two leaders discussed ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation in defence, security, trade and investment.
The Prime Minister also discussed regional and global issues of mutual interest with his counterparts from Singapore and Thailand on the sidelines of the visit.

Leaders of ‌the four-nation Quad grouping ⁠strongly oppose any destabilising or ‌unilateral actions that seek ‌to ‌change ⁠the status ⁠quo, including by force or coercion, which ‌escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and ‌stability, a joint statement said.
The leaders also ‌expressed grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary ‌export restrictions, the statement added after their ⁠meeting in Manila.

The Quad grouping, following its meeting in Manila, announced the ‘Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration’ which is “ a new initiative to enhance information sharing and maritime domain awareness”
“In 2027, our respective P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are scheduled to fly in a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, making our seas safer,” the statement added.

articles.title: India cannot dictate terms on Hasina’s return to Bangladesh: PM’s adviser
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Hasina has been staying in India since fleeing the country in August 2024 following a student-led uprising that toppled her government

Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Information Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) said that India or any other country could not dictate terms over deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s return home.
Hasina has been staying in India since fleeing the country in August 2024 following a student-led uprising that toppled her government.
Talking to reporters at the Bangladesh Secretariat, Mr. Zahed said, “Bangladesh is now an independent, sovereign state standing on firm legal ground and it will reject any unjust terms.”
The premier’s Adviser, however, said he did not believe India would attach conditions to returning Hasina.
On Friday (November 13, 2026), Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Hasina's extradition was a legal matter and would be dealt with accordingly.
He further said: “India desires a positive, constructive and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh."
Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal convicted Hasina in November 2025 of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown on protesters during the July-August 2024 uprising.
Tried in absentia, she was sentenced to death on one charge and life imprisonment on another. Hasina has rejected the charges and the proceedings.

In a report last week, BBC Bangla said unnamed Indian officials indicated that New Delhi set two main conditions to facilitate Hasina’s return amid Dhaka’s repeated insistence on her extradition under a bilateral treaty despite her repeated stated plan to return home voluntarily to face the legal procedure.
The report said that “under the conditions, India wanted Bangladesh Army to directly receive Hasina either via a military flight to Delhi or at a land border crossing”.

articles.title: ‘Record horticultural production’ shows increase of 4.36% from 2024-25: Agriculture Ministry
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Significant increase in horticultural production reflects the hard work of India’s farmers and the impact of the Centre’s farmer-friendly policies, Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan says

India’s total horticultural production is expected to reach 3,869.15 lakh tonnes in 2025-26, an increase of 161.77 lakh tonnes (4.36%) over the production recorded in 2024-25, according to the third advanced estimates of area and production of horticultural crops released by Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan in New Delhi on Tuesday (November 17, 2026). In the previous crop season, horticulture production stood at 3,707.38 lakh tonnes.

Mr. Chouhan expressed satisfaction over the projected growth and said the significant increase in horticultural production reflected the hard work of India’s farmers and the impact of the Union government’s farmer-friendly policies. “This record production would not only strengthen the country’s nutritional security but also directly contribute to higher incomes for horticulture farmers,” the Minister said, congratulating farmers across the country for their efforts.

Farmers were increasingly moving beyond traditional crops towards the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, and plantation crops, including cashew, coconut and cocoa, as well as aromatic and medicinal plants, he said.

“This growing interest in commercial and high-value crops is opening up new avenues of income for farmers while creating fresh opportunities for self-reliance and growth in the agricultural sector,” Mr. Chouhan said, adding that one of the most significant aspects of the latest estimates was increase in production despite a reduction in the area under horticultural cultivation.

“The total area under horticultural crops in 2025-26 is estimated at approximately 297.21 lakh hectares, compared with 301.36 lakh hectares in 2024-25. Despite the decline in cultivated area, production is projected to increase across fruits, vegetables, flowers, plantation crops, and aromatic and medicinal plants,” Mr. Chouhan said.

Fruit production is estimated to rise from 1,176.49 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 to 1,230.66 lakh tonnes in 2025-26, an increase of 54.18 lakh tonnes or 4.60%. “The improved output is primarily attributed to better production of banana, mango, papaya, apple, pomegranate and jackfruit,” the Union Agriculture Ministry said in a release.

The area under vegetables is estimated to increase from 117.91 lakh hectares to 119.31 lakh hectares. “Vegetable production is projected to rise by 4.35%, from 2,177.97 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 to 2,272.68 lakh tonnes in 2025-26. The increase is primarily driven by higher production of potato, tomato, brinjal, bottle gourd, cucumber, cabbage, beans and peas,” the release added. Potato and tomato production are both expected to register strong growth. Potato production is estimated at 655.70 lakh tonnes, up 11.95% from 585.71 lakh tonnes in the previous year. Tomato production is projected to increase from 205.99 lakh tonnes to 214.11 lakh tonnes. Onion production is estimated at 288.96 lakh tonnes.

Flower production is projected to rise by approximately 14.45%, from 42.65 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 to 48.82 lakh tonnes in 2025-26. “The area under flower cultivation has also increased to 4.10 lakh hectares,” it added. In the production of plantation crops, including arecanut, coconut, cashew, betel leaves and cocoa. “Their combined production is estimated to increase by 7.56% to 182.64 lakh tonnes. Production of aromatic and medicinal plants is also expected to rise from 9.01 lakh tonnes to 9.28 lakh tonnes,” the Ministry of Agriculture added.

The production of turmeric, garlic, curry leaves and cardamom is also expected to grow. “The total area under spices in 2025-26 is estimated at 47.56 lakh hectares, with production projected at 123.54 lakh tonnes,” the Ministry said.

articles.title: Microplastics, 'cocktail' of hazardous chemicals in Delhi's Yamuna, flags study
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The researchers also identified pharmaceutical compounds such as atomoxetine, domperidone and telmisartan, along with agrochemical-related substances, including diuron and thiamethoxam

Microplastics in the Yamuna in Delhi are accompanied by a complex mixture of organic chemicals, including pharmaceutical residues, pesticides and industrial effluents, with many of these substances classified as human-health and environmental hazards, according to a new study by University of Delhi researchers.

The study, published in the 'Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances ' in September 2026, examines microplastic pollution and associated chemical profiles at eight locations along a 48.8-km stretch of the river in Delhi -- from its entry at Palla to its exit at Asgarpur Jagir -- highlighting how pollution patterns vary across agricultural, residential, industrial, recreational and forested areas.

Researchers recovered 2,289 microplastic particles from the samples, with an average abundance of 3.18 particles per litre. The analysis identified 321 distinct chemical compounds across the samples, of which 50 were detected in extracts of recovered microplastic fractions at four or more locations.

Of these 50 compounds, 36 corresponded to structures with Global Harmonized System (GHS) hazard classifications, covering categories such as carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, acute toxicity and aquatic hazards.
Seven compounds were detected across all eight sampling locations, including 2-naphthylamine, lidocaine and monobutyl phthalate, the study found.
The researchers also identified pharmaceutical compounds such as atomoxetine, domperidone and telmisartan, along with agrochemical-related substances, including diuron and thiamethoxam.

Radhey Shyam Sharma, head of the Department of Environmental Studies at University of Delhi and one of the co-authors of the study, said the findings highlight the need to look beyond microplastic particles and examine the complex chemical mixtures present in river ecosystems.

"The microplastics problem, along with this cocktail of organic and inorganic substances, needs to be looked at through the lens of mixture toxicity. The land-use pattern has also been explored in the study," Sharma said.
He stressed the importance of nature-based solutions, including strengthening vegetation along riverbanks and protecting natural river ecosystems, to minimise pollution-related risks.

"Vegetation ecosystems can help prevent pollution from entering the river. Natural ecosystems and riverbanks need to be strengthened to minimise these risks. The focus should be on nature-based solutions," he said.

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time improves an already perfect classic
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: One of the best Zelda games, Ocarina of Time, has got a gorgeous new remake that is worth playing, if you have a Switch 2

Remakes of past games are pure genius. There are several titles that were mega hits in the 90s or early 2000s when both silicon and game engines were breaking new ground in 3D. Many of those games do not hold up today as well as the pixel game era of the NES and SNES eras do.

Capcom has shown the world that remaking most of their lineup of Resident Evils has been successful. Ubisoft did it too, with Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag Resynced . No one expected Nintendo to jump into the fray, but they did and with style, not only remaking a Zelda game, but one of the cult favorites from the Nintendo 64 era. A game so loved, that it is continuously ranked as one of the greatest games of all times, which is a risky move to remake.
Fortunately, the Ocarina of Time remake not only wears that crown proudly, but is also the only game this year to challenge the sales might of the neon clad tsunami that is Grand Theft Auto VI .

Another saga begins in the cyclic battle of good versus evil, and it revolves around the only boy in the village without a fairy. Entrusted with the fate of the world Link must stop the evil Ganondorf who is intent on grabbing the Tri-force — an artefact that grants the bearer immense power. Guided by the enigmatic fairy Navi, Link must leave the safety of his home, Kokiri Forest, and journey across the sprawling expanse of Hyrule Field, venturing through perilous dungeons, and shift between childhood and adulthood to claim the Master Sword and become the Hero of Time.

Jumping between time from Link’s adult self to his child form is so meta, it will make you feel like you too are jumping through time with him. As an adult, tethered by responsibilities of adulting, you get to jump back to your childhood — something that is more poignant than nostalgia.

In comparison to some of the more sweeping, complex narratives of today’s fantasy games, Ocarina of Time harks back to a simplistic form of storytelling, which was mostly due to cartridge size restrictions. However, it is a template that many of Zelda’s best games have been set on. First-time players are sure to find Link’s story a refreshing one that focuses on core gameplay mechanics and a beautiful reimagining of the world.

The world is gorgeous and while it is not quite open, it does feel like it has got a lot of freedom of movement. It is great to explore all the temples filled with its well-created puzzles that you may remember the solutions for and see the new renditions of iconic places such as Death Mountain, Hyrule Field, Temple of Time and other faithful to their original designs, but are now a lot more fleshed out.
Much of the world has a lot more detail. So rather than rushing through the game, take in your surroundings and scrutinise houses, because there is environmental storytelling peppered everywhere.

Much of the game has been faithfully translated, but thankfully it is free from the oddities of that N64 controller. In addition to updated control mechanics, there are a lot of quality of life improvements, and those who have played Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom , may find the controls familiar. The motions are fluid, and there are some physics-based systems at play, that make everything from the sword clashes feel solid to the sensation of things being physically there in the world as they bounce around.

Combat gains quality of life improvements, inheriting motion aiming from its predecessors making it more snappy, lively and reactive. It lets you acrobatically dodge, backflip and attack enemies, and hits do feel like they actually connect. The enemy AI and animations have been changed to make those fights all the more nail-biting. This being the Switch 2, there are also motion controls to help you use Hookshot, Longshots, bows for some more dynamic ranged combat, if you preferred using this in the newer Zelda games. The addition of jump mechanics do change the dungeons a bit, meaning instead of having the original jump in certain zones, now you actually have to platform across.

articles.title: Hospital in Chennai performs complex aortic surgery on 10-year-old boy with rare vascular disease
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The child recovered and was discharged on the ninth day after surgery

A 10-year-old with a rare inflammatory blood vessel disease underwent surgery at SIMS Hospital, Chennai, to repair a large aneurysm of the aortic arch, the hospital said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).

The patient was diagnosed with aortoarteritis, also known as Takayasu arteritis, a condition that causes inflammation and narrowing or enlargement of blood vessels. The aneurysm had enlarged significantly, causing breathing difficulty, palpitations, and difficulty lying down. The risk of rupture made urgent surgery necessary. The patient weighed about 18 kg, adding to the technical challenges of the operation. As the aneurysm was located close to the breastbone, opening the chest through the usual approach carried a risk of injuring the enlarged aorta. The surgical team first connected the patient to a heart-lung machine through blood vessels in the groin.

The patient has resumed normal activities without breathing difficulty but will require continued medication and monitoring to control the underlying inflammation and prevent further aneurysms.

articles.title: Assam elephant rescue operation turns violent, eight people arrested
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The incident occurred when Forest personnel tried to guide a female elephant, separated from a herd, back to the jungle it came from

Eight people were detained in central Assam’s Hojai district after they clashed with Forest Department personnel on Monday night (November 16, 2026) during an operation to guide a female elephant back to the jungle it came from.

The Forest officials fired “sera bullets” (pellets) from a pump-action gun to divert the elephant away from a human settlement. Five people were injured in the firing, triggering the mob violence and leaving two personnel injured.
Forest officials claimed three people sustained pellet injuries. The injured, including one of the two personnel, were admitted to a local hospital for treatment.

Divisional Forest Officer Nayan Jyoti Rajbongshi said a herd of elephants from the hills of Karbi Anglong entered the Hawaipur Reserve Forest in Hojai on Monday morning. Barring the female elephant, estimated to be 40 years old, the herd returned to Karbi Anglong a few hours later.
“We received information about the movement of the female elephant, possibly separated from the herd, along a road in a revenue area. We managed to push it into the Hawaipur Reserve Forest,” he said.
However, the elephant emerged from the forest around dusk and headed toward a village. The Forest personnel fired the pellets to drive it away, but some villagers were injured in the process.
“The police brought the situation under control and picked up eight people who clashed with our personnel. The police recorded the statement of our personnel,” Mr. Rajbongshi said.
Wildlife officials said people often obstruct rescue operations by gathering around a wild animal that strays out of a forest.
According to Assam government data tabled in the 126-member Assembly in July, as many as 1,147 people and 246 elephants were killed in human-elephant conflicts in the State since 2016.

articles.title: Chinese scientist fired after child death in gene-editing trial: state media
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report
A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a six-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been sacked following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition -- which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.

Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature , according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch .

Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on February 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity", the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was sacked and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.

A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a six-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been sacked following a government probe, according to state media.

The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition -- which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.

Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature , according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch .

Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.

The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on February 18.

Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity", the report said.

Another researcher on Qiu's team was sacked and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.

The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.

The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.

The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.

articles.title: Clear the path: On SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India should use multilateral fora to advance bilateral cooperation

While maintaining its hard stance on cross-border terrorism, India has an opportunity to recognise that many of its other interests still merit sustained cooperation with Pakistan as the latter’s climate minister Musadik Masood Malik prepares to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi. India’s official position since the Pahalgam attack and the ensuing confrontations along the border is that terrorism and bilateral talks cannot coexist. A month later, Prime Minister Narendra Modi signalled that India’s relations with Pakistan would remain subordinate to its demands on cross-border terrorism by extending the condition to trade and water. South Asia is already one of the least economically integrated regions worldwide, with intra-regional trade at around 5%, and, as Chatham House has inferred, strained ties between India and its neighbours have created diplomatic vacuums that Beijing has taken advantage of through trilateral and regional groupings. Now, by inviting all SCO members to the national capital and participating in meetings ahead of the August 2027 Islamabad Summit, New Delhi has shown some maturity as a convening power. Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Mr. Modi.

The pursuit of regionwide water security remains particularly fluid, with India seemingly overlooking the fact that it is upstream of Pakistan and Bangladesh and downstream of China. After India stopped sharing routine hydrological data of the Indus river and approved the Chenab-Beas link tunnel project, Mr. Malik fanned the flames saying Pakistan would “cut off those hands” seeking to restrict its share of the water. Yet China has now restricted the same data vis-à-vis the Brahmaputra while it builds the Medog mega-dam in Tibet. India has also protested the proposed Padma Barrage in Bangladesh, which has been increasing its alignment with China, echoing India building the Farakka Barrage over East Pakistan’s objections in 1961. Climate change is rendering cooperation more essential to manage the integrity of contested geographies, the willingness of border populations to engage, and the potential to generate hydroelectric power. New Delhi should retreat from the notion that working together on the Indus will be a concession to Islamabad and see in the Dialogue an opportunity to restore the necessary channels. Suspending ties may communicate political resolve but will not diminish terrorists’ capabilities in the region or improve India’s security. It has already compromised India’s ambitions to regional leadership, which require the ability to keep engaging even with difficult neighbours. India should go beyond using multilateral fora to assert its national position and start identifying areas where bilateral cooperation serves its interests, including with Pakistan.

articles.title: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The dangers of centralising the internet’s architecture are now clear

Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

The dangers of centralising the internet’s architecture are now clear

Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

articles.title: Brace for impact: On rising inflation and external factors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: High inflation due to external factors could soon exacerbate economic pain

India’s much-hyped domestic economic resilience is set to be tested over the next few months as external factors start to impose inescapable pressures. A case in point is inflation. The latest data on retail inflation show that it crossed the Reserve Bank of India’s 6% upper comfort limit in October 2026. According to economists, this is likely to continue through the third quarter of this financial year, which means at least two more months of high inflation. Agricultural shortfalls brought on by a patchy and deficient monsoon have meant that food inflation rose sharply to 8.5% in October 2026. Elevated fuel prices meant that inflation in the transport category also rose sharply. What is worse is that high inflation is spreading to almost every aspect of a household’s day-to-day needs. In fact, the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) data show that 10 of the 12 major categories saw inflation in October, hitting their highest levels recorded in the new series of the index. So, things such as clothing, footwear, housing, furnishings, and services such as healthcare, education, communication, recreation, and restaurant and hospitality are not only getting more expensive, but they are doing so at an accelerating rate. This would have been bad enough had wages been increasing in real terms. Yet, the latest research by Data for India on the country’s official wage statistics shows that, while nominal wages doubled from 2012 to 2024, they actually fell 4% over the same period after adjusting for inflation. And this is sharper for high-skilled and high-earning workers. Lower wage earners saw marginal increases over this period. While this is of some comfort, it is the higher wage earners that drive consumption in an economy. Real wage contraction for them, which is likely to have worsened in 2026, will hit consumption levels and private investment.

Further, there is strong evidence to suggest that the official inflation metrics are not capturing the full extent of rising prices. Data on cash with the public and UPI transactions show the value of both has been growing in double digits over the last year and more, significantly outpacing nominal GDP growth. This either suggests that the informal economy is far larger than earlier thought or, more likely, that inflation is well above what the official figures are being able to capture. Unfortunately, there are no real magic-wand fixes to this situation. Inflation is largely beyond the government’s control, and wage growth cannot happen overnight. The only way forward is to continue trying to spur sector-specific growth and warn people of the impending storm.
